newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economic recovery becoming more solid - BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Japan economic recovery becoming more solid - BOJ.

text.p: Japan's economic recovery appears to be becoming more solid, as seen in the central bank's recent "tankan" survey, Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference on Monday.
"The economy is continuing to recover gradually. The strength of the economic recovery appears to be becoming more solid," he said.
The BOJ governor spoke on the first day of a two-day trip to western Japan.
Matsushita explained the tankan survey of corporate sentiment for November released last week supported his view on the economy.
The tankan's diffusion index of corporate sentiment showed that the pace of improvement was still gradual and differed according to sectors, he said.
However, other factors, such as the outlooks for corporate profits and capital spending, supported his view that the economic recovery was becoming more solid, he said.
Private consumption was starting to gradually recover again after stalling in the summer and corporate capital spending was also improving, he said.
A decline in net exports had taken a breather after the correction of the yen's strength since last year and stock adjustment in materials industries was proceeding, he said.
"The pace of the rise in industrial production is becoming quicker after moving sideways in the first half of the year," he said.
However, companies had not dropped their cautious stance towards future prospects due to pressures from structural adjustments and an expected drop in public investment, Matsushita added.
"We can well expect a favourable economic cycle of production creating income and then consumption to strengthen further. However we still need to make sure this is on track," Matsushita said.
Asked about the BOJ's monetary policy, Matsushita said: "We will put emphasis on ensuring a basis for economic recovery while keeping close watch on economic conditions."

Matsushita said that the central bank's easy money policy was intended to prevent a deflationary spiral, to strengthen corporate confidence and to put the economy back on a self-sustainable recovery track.
He said that the first two aims had "just about been achieved".

Asked about the effects of currency market movements on Japan's economy, Matsushita said that the correction of the strong yen had slowed down the shrinking trend of Japan's current account surplus and pushed up corporate profits.
Although the prices of imports had moved up somewhat, this factor had not created inflation in overall domestic prices because of loose supply and demand conditions in Japan, he said.
Matsushita said that the series of problems at financial firms was regrettable but quick dealing with such problems would lead to a recovery in the credibility of the Japanese financial system.
Matsushita also said that he did not think that there would be any problem in securing liquidity for creditors of recently failed Hanwa Bank.
He said that with the recent passage of financial bills, Japan was better equipped to cope with financial failures.

The governor added that Japan's economy was being pulled by two forces -- one, a favourable economic cycle which would move the economy upwards and the other, pressure from structural adjustment which was holding back economic recovery.

He said that structural-adjustment pressures included the need to improve corporate balance sheets, which worsened after the bursting of the bubble economy, and increasing competition from developing countries.
Both factors were making companies push restructuring efforts, he said.
